rows.name: fifo-why
rows.question: Why does index equality alone not distinguish full from empty? Give the two concrete capacity-17 states and show how your actual implementation distinguishes them.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Why does index equality alone not distinguish full from empty? Give the two concrete capacity-17 states and show how your actual implementation distinguishes them.
rows.answer:
Index equality alone is ambiguous because both zero queued items and 17 queued items put the tail at the head after modulo-17 wrapping.

Initially, the concrete state is head_ = 0, tail_ = 0, size_ = 0: empty() is true, full() is false, and pop rejects without changing anything. After pushing values 0 through 16, the state is head_ = 0, tail_ = 0, size_ = 17: empty() is false, full() is true, and the next push rejects without changing anything.

The actual implementation distinguishes those states using size_. Its invariant is 0 ≤ size_ ≤ 17 and tail_ = (head_ + size_) modulo 17, so all 17 slots are usable without reserving an empty slot.

review.note: Actual empty0/0/size0 and full0/0/size17 correctly distinguished by size; tail=(head+size)%17.
review.usefulPrefix: Index equality alone is ambiguous because both zero queued items and 17 queued items put the tail at the head after modulo-17 wrapping.

rows.name: floating-counterexample
rows.question: Under IEEE binary32, round after each addition and forbid reassociation. Evaluate (16777216 + -16777216) + 1 and 16777216 + (-16777216 + 1). Then change the leftmost operand to positive 16777216, the middle operand to 1, and the last operand to -16777216. Compare both parenthesizations of that changed triple. Explain representability at each intermediate step; do not simply cite nonassociativity.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Under IEEE binary32, round after each addition and forbid reassociation. Evaluate (16777216 + -16777216) + 1 and 16777216 + (-16777216 + 1). Then change the leftmost operand to positive 16777216, the middle operand to 1, and the last operand to -16777216. Compare both parenthesizations of that changed triple. Explain representability at each intermediate step; do not simply cite nonassociativity.
rows.answer:
Assuming IEEE’s default round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, the original expressions both equal 1; the changed triple gives 0 with left grouping and 1 with right grouping.

Original triple:
• (16777216 + -16777216) + 1: cancellation gives exactly 0, then exactly 1. Both intermediates are representable.
• 16777216 + (-16777216 + 1): the inner result is exactly -16777215, which is representable; the outer sum is exactly 1.

Changed triple:
• (16777216 + 1) + -16777216: the exact inner sum, 16777217, is not representable. At this magnitude, adjacent binary32 values are 16777216 and 16777218. It is halfway between them, so ties-to-even rounds to 16777216; the final addition then gives exactly 0.
• 16777216 + (1 + -16777216): the inner sum is exactly -16777215, which is representable; the final sum is exactly 1.

The crucial boundary is 16777216 = 2^24: spacing is 1 immediately below that positive magnitude and 2 immediately above it. Thus -16777215 is representable, while 16777217 is not.

review.note: Explicit round-to-nearest ties-even assumption; original both1, changed0versus1; representability and spacing on each side of2^24 correctly proved.
review.usefulPrefix: Assuming IEEE’s default round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, the original expressions both equal 1; the changed triple gives 0 with left grouping and 1 with right grouping.

rows.name: quorum-counterexample
rows.question: Five replicas A,B,C,D,E retain the highest version. A writer finishes after three acknowledgements. A reader queries any three and returns the highest version, without write-back. Prove or disprove linearizability including reads overlapping an incomplete write: give a fully ordered execution with two nonoverlapping reads and show the attempted linearization contradiction. Then change only the reader to write the selected version to three replicas before returning and explain whether this fixes the counterexample.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Five replicas A,B,C,D,E retain the highest version. A writer finishes after three acknowledgements. A reader queries any three and returns the highest version, without write-back. Prove or disprove linearizability including reads overlapping an incomplete write: give a fully ordered execution with two nonoverlapping reads and show the attempted linearization contradiction. Then change only the reader to write the selected version to three replicas before returning and explain whether this fixes the counterexample.
rows.answer:
Without write-back, the protocol is not linearizable: two nonoverlapping reads can return a new version and then an older one.

Start with version 0 on all five replicas. Here is a fully ordered execution:
1. The writer invokes a write of version 1.
2. A stores version 1 and acknowledges. Messages to B,C,D,E are delayed, so the write remains incomplete.
3. Read R1 starts, queries A,B,C, and receives versions 1,0,0.
4. R1 returns version 1.
5. After R1 finishes, read R2 starts and queries B,C,D. All three return version 0.
6. R2 returns version 0.
7. Finally, the delayed write reaches B and C. They acknowledge, and the writer finishes with three acknowledgements.

To justify R1’s result, the write of version 1 must be linearized before R1. Real-time ordering requires R1 before R2, so the attempted order is write 1 → R1 → R2. With no intervening write, R2 cannot return version 0. Placing the write after R1 instead makes R1’s return impossible. An incomplete write may be placed within its invocation interval, but no placement resolves this contradiction.

Requiring read write-back fixes this counterexample. Before R1 returns version 1, it must receive acknowledgements from three replicas that have stored version 1 or higher. Any three replicas queried by R2 intersect that write-back quorum, since 3 + 3 > 5. Because replicas never decrease their versions, R2 must observe and return at least version 1. Delayed older messages cannot undo this.

With a single writer assigning increasing versions, this is the standard atomic quorum-register approach: even a read that discovers an incomplete write makes its selected version durable on a majority before returning. For multiple writers, write-back still prevents this counterexample, but a full linearizability guarantee additionally requires a correct, unique, totally ordered version-assignment protocol; that is not specified here.

review.note: Fully ordered pending A-only version1 write, R1ABC1 then nonoverlapping R2BCD0 then write completion establishes inversion; W<R1<R2 contradiction. Readwriteback majority intersection fixes counterexample; singlewriter increasing/multiwriter unique-version qualification retained.
review.usefulPrefix: Without write-back, the protocol is not linearizable: two nonoverlapping reads can return a new version and then an older one.

rows.name: quorum-why
rows.question: Why does the second read have to respect a value returned by the first read even if the writer never completed? State the relevant real-time order and distinguish it from requiring every unfinished operation to complete.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Why does the second read have to respect a value returned by the first read even if the writer never completed? State the relevant real-time order and distinguish it from requiring every unfinished operation to complete.
rows.answer:
Because the first read completed before the second read began, linearizability requires the first read to precede the second in the sequential explanation. If the first read returns version 1, the pending write of version 1 must be included and ordered before that read; with no intervening write, the second read cannot then return version 0.

The required order is write(1) → read₁ returning 1 → read₂, where read₁’s response occurs before read₂’s invocation. This does not require every unfinished operation to actually complete: a linearizability check may omit pending operations or supply hypothetical responses to include them. But this particular write cannot be omitted, because then nothing explains the first read’s value.

review.note: R1 response before R2 invocation forces real-time order; pending write must be included to explain observed1, but hypothetical completion does not require all actual unfinished operations to finish.
review.usefulPrefix: Because the first read completed before the second read began, linearizability requires the first read to precede the second in the sequential explanation.
